﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾

What has preceded regarding its counterparts (naẓā'ir) has already been stated.

**[Verse 2]** ﴿The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The surah opens by extolling the Qur'an, because it is the comprehensive guidance that this surah and others contain. Moreover, the root of the misguidance of the astray is denial of this Book. God made the Qur'an a guidance for mankind and honored the Arabs by making them the first to receive this Book, and by revealing it in their language. Yet among them were the most fierce deniers of what it brought. Undoubtedly, the denial of those deniers is deeper in error and more extreme in perversity of opinion.

The opening of the speech with a nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) indicates permanence and stability.

The subject (al-musnad ilayh) is introduced as a definite noun through an annexation (idafah), because of its length. Through this lengthening, and then following it with the parenthetical clause (al-jumlah al-mu'taridah), the aim is to create suspense about knowing the predicate, which is his saying ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾. Were it not for this, it would have been said: "A Qur'an sent down from the Lord of the worlds," or something similar.

The reason for departing from the style of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1] ﴿This is the Book, in which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah is that that surah was revealed among the Muslims and among the People of the Book whose conversion was hoped for, and they are ﴿those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4]. As for this surah, God confronted with it the polytheists who do not believe in the One God and do not have certainty about the Hereafter; they are more stubborn and greater in disbelief and aversion.

So his saying ﴿revelation of the Book﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and his saying ﴿in which there is no doubt﴾ is a clause that is either an attribute of the Book, or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah).

[Page 206]

His saying ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is the predicate (khabar) concerning the subject, and "min" here is for origin (ibtida'iyyah).

The meaning is: from His presence and His revelation, just as you say: "A book came to me from so-and-so." The clause ﴿in which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] is in the style of what is known and established, so it was not made a second predicate of the subject, in order to increase the suspense toward the predicate, to affirm that it is from the Lord of the worlds.

The meaning of ﴿in which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] is that it is not fit for anyone to doubt its revelation from the Lord of the worlds, because of the decisive proofs surrounding its revelation that it is not from the speech of humans, by reason of the inimitability of even the shortest surah of it, let alone the whole of it, and what supports it from the condition of the one to whom it was sent, namely his well-known truthfulness and uprightness, and the coming of its like from one like him (i.e. an unlettered man), together with what is known of the attribute of being unlettered (al-ummiyyah).

So the meaning of negating that doubt be contained within this Book is that it does not include anything that stirs doubt. Those who doubted, or rather denied, that it is from God are either stubborn people acting with knowledge, or ignorant people who speak before they reflect and wait. The former are their leaders and the latter their common folk. This was already mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The mention of the Majesty (al-Jalalah) by way of annexation, through the description "Lord of the worlds," rather than by the proper name or other means of definition, is because it indicates the universality of the Law and that its Book is revealed for all people, unlike the previous divine books, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book and as a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. It also indicates that among the causes of their denial of it is their resentment, saying in their own selves: how did God choose for His message a man from among them? For the lordship of God over the worlds indicates that He cannot be questioned about what He does, and that He knows best where to place His messages.

[Page 207]

Here *am* (أم) is used to turn away from the preceding discourse, a turning to a new subject (*idrab intiqal*, "transitional turning away"). It is the disjunctive *am* (*umm al-munqati'ah*), which has the sense of *bal* ("rather"), the particle of change of topic (*li-al-idtirab*).

Wherever *am* occurs, it indicates an interrogative with the hamzah (*istifham*) that follows it, and that hamzah is obligatorily omitted after *am*. The interrogative implied here is one of wonder (*ta'jibi*), because they uttered this shocking statement and people knew it of them. Therefore they deserve to be wondered at for their condition and their saying, since with it they displayed a strange matter that calls for astonishment among the intelligent, the people of sound judgement and the fair-minded. The signs that doubt about its being from the Lord of the worlds is absent are clear, to say nothing of the certainty that it is an invention against God Most High.

The report of their astonishing saying is expressed in the present tense (*al-mudari'*) to bring the state of that saying before the mind, to make the wonder at it vivid, so that the hearers do not lose sight of the situation of their saying. This is like the word "she says" (*taqulu*) in the verse of Hudhul al-'Anbari, one of the poets of the *Hamasah* anthology:

*She says, and strikes her breast with her hand: "Is this my husband, with the hindering millstone?"*

The present tense, moreover, signals that their saying is renewed and that they do not desist from it despite the clear signs that have come to them, and despite their exposure through their inability to match it.

The pronoun in *iftarahu* ("he has invented it") refers to the Prophet ﷺ, since this is known from the context of reporting their widely known saying among the people. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the Book.

They are rebutted by *bal* ("rather") in the sense of nullification (*idrab ibtal*): ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, to establish that the Qur'an is true. The meaning of *al-haqq* ("the truth") is truthfulness, that is, in what it contains, of which one aspect is that it is sent down from God Most High. The definiteness of *al-haqq* is the definiteness of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), which affirms the realisation of genus in it.

That is: this truth, whose quiddity is known among all genera and which is distinct from the genus of falsehood, is true. Defining the predicate with the genus-article carries a hint that the perfection of this genus is attributed to the subject, and this is the meaning of the ascriptive restriction (*qasr idda'i*) for emphasis, as in the verse:

*You are the beloved, and 'Amr is the knight.*

*From your Lord* is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) relating to *al-haqq*. The truth that comes from God is, without doubt, the most perfect kind of truth. The *ka* of "your" is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. The exalted Essence is brought to mind here through the title "your Lord" because the discourse came as a reply to their saying "he has invented it", meaning the Prophet ﷺ. So the context of rebuttal called for confirming those whom they attached to a thing from which he is innocent, by establishing that the Book is the truth from the Lord of the one to whom they attributed invention. This honours the Messenger, peace be upon him, and leads on to affirming his truthfulness, since if the Book he brought is true and from God, then he is truly the Messenger of God.

This verse comes in a style of wondrous precision. It has been established that the Book is a revelation from the Lord of all created beings, and that it is fitting that no doubter should doubt it. Then the discourse moves to denunciation and wonder at those who were certain that the one who brought it is a fabricator against God. Then it rebutted them by establishing that it is the perfect truth from the Lord of the one they attributed invention to. Had he invented it, God would have been able to expose him, as God Most High said: ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:44] ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [69:45] ﴿Then We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [69:46] ﴿And not one of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ [69:47].

Then it brought what is more painful to the deniers, more eloquent in exposing the folly of their minds, and more profound in calling out their neglect of considering the subtleties of meanings. It made clear what is in it of reminder for them, through some of the benefits for which this Book came, by His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, so that they may be guided﴾. They had gathered in ignorance what is like a bundle of sticks upon a heap of bundles. For this Book, even apart from its being true, which calls for eagerness to benefit from it, even if they had not turned to its being hung upon them, and even though they had invited to taking it up, which obliges reflection on its truth, all of this considered: they were more in need of following it than the Jews, Christians and Magians. These had not been preceded by the message of any messenger, so they were further from the paths of guidance because of the generations that succeeded one another upon them without the call of a messenger. This was sufficient to make them eager to hold fast to it and aware of their greater need for it, in hope that they might be guided. God Most High said: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-An'am 6:155] ﴿Lest you say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [6:156] ﴿Or say, "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them?﴾ [6:157]. So the likeness of these deniers is like the saying of al-Ma'arri:

*Will the message of a messenger restrain you, or does it avail nothing with those who are far gone?*

*The people* (*al-qawm*): the great group whom a matter binds together, which serves as their foundation, whether a common lineage, a homeland, or an aim for which they gathered. Its most common use is for a group who trace their lineage to a forefather whom they alone claim as their ancestor, and who are thereby distinguished from those who share with them a more distant ancestor. Thus Quraysh, for example, is a people who have singled themselves out by ascribing themselves to Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, and they became distinguished from the other descendants of Kinanah. So one says: "So-and-so is a Qurashi, and so-and-so is a Kinani", but no one from among the sons of Quraysh is called a Kinani.

The people are described as those ﴿to whom no warner had come﴾ [al-Qasas 28:46] before the Prophet ﷺ, at a time when he was calling the people of Makkah and its surroundings to Islam, and perhaps the call included the people of Yathrib too, and all of them were Arabs. It is therefore clear that the intended people are the Arabs to whom no messenger had come before Muhammad, peace be upon him. This may mean Quraysh specifically, or the Arabs of the Hijaz, the people of Makkah and Madinah and the tribes of the Hijaz. The Arabs of the Hijaz are of two stocks: the Adnanites and the Qahtanites. As for the Adnanites, they are the sons of 'Adnan, who are of the progeny of Isma'il. Their nationhood was formed among the sons of 'Adnan: Mudar, Rabi'ah, Anmar and Iyad. None of these had received a messenger since their nationhood took shape.

As for their forefather Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, although he was a messenger and prophet, as God Most High described him in Surat Maryam, his mission was specifically to his family and in-laws from Jurhum. He was not sent to those who came after him, because his mission was neither lasting nor widespread. God Most High said: ﴿And he used to enjoin his people to prayer and zakah﴾ [Maryam 19:55].

As for the Qahtanites who dwelt in the Hijaz, such as the Aws, the Khazraj and Tayy, their groups and homelands changed after the flood of al-'Arim, and they divided into new peoples. No warner had come to them since that time, although warners had come to their ancestors, such as Hud, Salih and Tubba'. That was before their new nationhood took shape.

Or the intended people may be all the Arabs, including the people of Yemen, Yamamah, Bahrain and others covered by the Arabian Peninsula. All of them trace back to these two stocks, and their division into peoples and homelands occurred after the flood of al-'Arim. No warner had come to them after that division, as already explained concerning the Qahtanites of the Hijaz. As for what is reported about Hanzalah ibn Safwan, the companion of the people of al-Rass, and Khalid ibn Sinan, the companion of Banu 'Abs, it is not established that they were messengers, and their prophethood is disputed. It has been reported that the daughter of Khalid ibn Sinan came to the Prophet ﷺ while she was an old woman, and he said to her: "Welcome, daughter of a prophet whom his people neglected." But there is no sound chain for this.

Whichever of these is meant, all the Arabs, or those covered by the call of Islam on that day, are rightly described as those ﴿to whom no warner had come﴾ from the time their nationhood was realised.

The purpose of this is to remind them that they are the people most in need of a warner, since they were not upon any remnant of guidance. It also stirs their aspirations, so that they may envy the People of the Book, accept the Book sent down to them, and precede the People of the Book in following it. Thus the believers will have precedence from it in the final law, just as those among the People of the Book who did not embrace Islam had precedence through some guidance and through practising the earlier Book. Some of the wise men of the Arabs were concerned to seek the true religion: many Arabs of Yemen became Jews, Tayy, Kalb, Taghlib and others among the Arab Christians became Christians, and some followed the *hanifiyyah* (primordial monotheism), such as Qss ibn Sa'idah, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. This was a quest for perfection, and no messenger had come to them with it.

This reasoning does not require that the Islamic message be restricted to these people, nor does it contradict the universality of the message for those to whom a warner has come. For the particle of cause (*lam al-'illah*) requires only that what follows it be a motive for the occurrence of the act to which it is attached, not that the motive of the act be confined to that cause. A single act may have many motives, and the acts of God Most High are bound to numerous wisdoms. The proofs of the universality of the message are abundant, from the clear text of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and from the universality of the call.

It has been said: the people to whom no warner had come before are all the nations, and that what is meant by "no warner had come to them" is that none had come to them after they went astray, whether those who went astray within their law, like the People of the Book, or those who went astray by being devoid of any law, like the Arabs. But this view is remote from the wording *qawm* ("people") and from the verb *atahum* ("came to them"), and it defeats the purpose of this description as we have already explained.

As for the question of the universality of the Muhammadan call, its proofs are many, apart from this verse.

Perhaps the expression is a metaphor, depicting the intent for their guidance and the eagerness for its attainment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 4:

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne. You have, besides Him, no protector and no intercessor. Will you not then remember?﴾

Since the greatest pillar among the pillars of the Book's guidance is the affirmation of the oneness of God (tawhid al-uluhiyya) and the negation of association (ibtal al-shirk), it comes right after the praise of the Book, through the establishment of this pillar.

The Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala), Allah, is placed as the subject (mubtada') so that it is brought to mind through the name specific to Him, definitively cutting off the root of the belief in a partner in divinity. The predicate of the subject is the clause ﴿You have, besides Him, no protector and no intercessor﴾, and His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 59] is an attribute of the Name of Majesty.

The relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) is used to indicate the reason for the predicate's construction, namely that He alone holds lordship (al-infirad bil-rububiyya) over all creatures in the heavens, the earth and whatever is between them, and among them are the polytheists, who are the intended ones by the predicate. The address is directed to the polytheists by way of iltifat (shift of discourse).

Al-waliyy (protector) is derived from al-wala' in the sense of covenant, alliance and kinship. Among the necessary implications of the true meaning of wala' is support and defence of the one who is protected (al-mawla). By al-waliyy is meant the one who shares in lordship.

Al-shafi' (intercessor) is the mediator in the fulfilment of needs, whether by averting harm or bringing benefit.

The polytheists claimed that the idols are gods, partners of Allah in divinity, and then said ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], and said ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3].

The min in His saying (min duniHi) is initial (ibtida'iyya) and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in lakum; duna means ghayr (other than). The min in His saying (min waliyy) is superfluous (za'ida), to emphasize the negation, meaning: you have no protector and no intercessor other than Allah. Thus there is no wilaya for the idols and no shafa'a for them, a negation that returns to negating divinity from them, as their claimed two attributes for their idols are refuted.

The meaning is not that they have no helper or intercessor except Allah, because Allah does not help them against Himself nor intercede for them with Himself. Allah the Exalted said ﴿That is because Allah is the protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11], and He said ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqara: 255].

The exegesis of its counterpart has already preceded: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days,

then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], and the explanation of the interpretation (ta'wil) of ﴿then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] is in Surat al-A'raf.

As a consequence of this proof comes a rebuke for their failure to reflect on this and their neglect of consideration, in His saying (a-fa-la tatadhakkarun) "Will you not then remember?", which is an interrogative of denunciation (istifham inkari). Al-tadhakkur is derived from al-dhikr, which is with a dammah on the dhal, and it means reflection and consideration by the intellect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 5:

﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.﴾

The clause (yudabbiru al-amr) (He arranges the affair) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah: 4], meaning: He created those creatures while arranging their affair. It is also possible that the clause is a new, independent statement (isti'naf). His saying (min al-sama') (from the heaven) is connected to (yudabbiru) (He arranges), or is a description of (al-amr) (the affair), or is a circumstantial clause from it. (Min) here indicates the starting point (ibtida'iyyah). The purpose of the two particles of beginning and end is the comprehensiveness of God the Exalted's arrangement of all affairs in the upper and lower worlds, an arrangement encompassing them from the heaven to the earth. Thus the particle of end (ila) conveys that His arrangement includes the affairs of everything in the heavens and the earth and what is between them.

Tadbir (arrangement): its true meaning is thinking about the issuing of an action perfected at its beginning and its end. It is derived from dubur al-amr (the back, i.e., the end, of the matter), because tadbir is the consideration of the rectitude of an action from beginning to end. When it is attributed to God the Exalted, it is a metonymy (kinayah) for its necessary consequence, which is the perfection of mastery. Something of this was mentioned at the beginning of Surah Yunus and at the beginning of Surah al-Ra'd.

Al-amr (the affair): the matter, the state of things, their order and that by which they are sustained. The definite article in it is for the genus, and it conveys the encompassing of all affairs; nothing among them lies outside His disposal. Therefore, everything reported from the earlier exegetes regarding the interpretation of al-amr returns to some part of this generality.

Al-'uruj: ascending. The pronoun in (ya'ruju) refers to (al-amr), and its transitivity with the particle of end (ila) conveys that those arranged affairs ascend to God the Exalted. Thus 'uruj here is used metaphorically for the return to the disposal of the Creator alone, without any admixture of influence from others, even apparently, as in the states of this world from the influence of causes. Since majesty (jalal) is likened to elevation in ordinary speech, the return to the Possessor of Majesty was likened to the movement of beings to a high place, which is expressed in the language as 'uruj, as God the Exalted said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], meaning: He raises it to Himself.

(Thumma) (then) indicates a graded sequence (tarakhi al-rutbi), because the return of things to His disposal after their issuance from Him is greater and more wondrous.

The construction conveys that the arrangement of affairs from the heaven to the earth, from the time of their creation and the creation of what is between them, remains settled upon what it has been arranged upon, each according to what the state of its arrangement requires of its stability; some of it passes away and some of it remains for as long as the heavens and the earth endure. Then He gathers all of that together, and it goes back to God in a return suited to its realities: essences go to the fate of essences, and accidents and deeds go to the fate of their like, i.e., their attribute and the attribute of their possessors go to the knowledge of God and the determination of recompense. That return is what is expressed as 'uruj to God, and so reckoning will be upon all created beings on that day.

The day in His saying: ﴿in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years﴾ is the day mentioned in the verse of Surah al-Hajj in His saying: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

The meaning of its measure being a thousand years is that there occurs in it, from God's disposals in the beings of the heavens and the earth, what would, if it were from the work of people, require the occurrence of its like over a thousand years. So you may estimate that by the multitude of dispositions, or by the covering of distances, and several possibilities have been suggested for this. The purpose is to alert to the greatness of power and the vastness of God's dominion and arrangement. It appears that this day is the Day of the Hour, that is, the hour of the dissolution of the worldly world; and the day mentioned here is not the Day of Resurrection mentioned in Surah al-Ma'arij; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

He did not specify either of them, and it is not the purpose of the reciters to specify which of the two days is meant, but rather that the lesson is attained through the terrors of both.

His saying (fi yawm) (in a Day) is governed by both verbs (yudabbiru) and (ya'ruju), meaning: both matters occur in a day.

(Alf) (a thousand) among the Arabs is the upper limit of the number names, and what exceeds that among counted things is expressed by other numbers together with the number of the thousand, as they say: five thousands (khamsatu alaf), a hundred thousand (mi'atu alf), and a million (alfu alf).

(Alf) may be used as a metaphor (kinayah) for intense multiplicity, as one says: "I visited you a thousand times," and as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96]. Here it is with an implied particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) or the word "nahwa" (approximately), meaning: its measure was like a thousand years or approximately a thousand years, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

It is also possible that (alf) is used in its literal meaning. His saying: "of what you count" means: of what you reckon in your counting. (Ma) here is either a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (mawsuliyyah), and the phrase is a description of "a thousand years." This description does not require that the name alf be used in its literal meaning, because it may serve as clarification of the comparison, and so it is close to mentioning the aspect of resemblance together with the comparison. It may also be preferred that this description, since it has the sense of the described noun, functions as a verbal emphasis of its signified meaning, and so it removes the possibility of metaphor in the number.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 6:

﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah, "that") is used to refer to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah, Allah), after the attributes of acting in creating beings and governing their affairs have been mentioned. This is to draw attention to the fact that the one referred to by the demonstrative deserves what follows the demonstrative because of those preceding attributes, as occurred in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Luqman: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah. Without doubt, the one who acts with that creation and governance knows all His creatures and encompasses all their conditions. Thus He is "Knower of the unseen," meaning what is hidden from the senses of creatures, and "Knower of the witnessed," meaning what falls under the perception of the senses. So "the unseen" and "the witnessed" mean every hidden thing and every observed thing.

The intended meaning is knowledge of the unseen, because when they denied resurrection and the revival of the dead, their doubt about its impossibility was that the parts of bodies had dispersed and mixed into the earth. For this reason, He followed it immediately with His saying (﴿And they say: "When we have strayed into the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [As-Sajdah: 10]). As for the conjunction of "and the witnessed," it is a completion (takmil) and a precautionary safeguard (ihtiras).

The reason for describing Him, exalted is He, as "the Almighty, the Most Merciful" right after what preceded is that He created creation by the sheer power of His own ability, without any helper. Thus the might (al-'izzah), which is self-sufficiency from others, is evident. Also, He created them in states that contain gentleness toward them, so He is Merciful to them in what He created, since He made the affairs of their lives suitable for them, containing bliss for them, and kept pain away from them. This is the reason for combining the two attributes "the Almighty" and "the Most Merciful" here, contrary to the usual pattern of mentioning "the All-Wise" alongside "the Almighty."

The phrases "the Almighty, the Most Merciful" may be two further predicates about the demonstrative, or two descriptive attributes of "Knower of the unseen."

Page 215

Another report about the demonstrative (ism al-ishara, "that"), or another description of "Knower of the unseen." It is an ascent in argument, mixed with a reminder of favour to people: that He perfected their creation as part of the perfection of the creation of everything, and by singling out the creation of man for mention. The intended meaning is that He is the One who created everything, and especially man, creating him after he was not a thing worth mentioning, and brought his origin out of dust, then arranged within him the system of reproduction from water. How, then, would the re-creation of his parts be beyond Him?

Ihsan (excellence, "perfecting") means making a thing good, that is, praiseworthy and free of defect. This is achieved when a thing fulfils the purpose for which it exists. When you reflect on things, you find them made as they ought to be: the firmness of the earth, for example, for walking upon it; the lightness of the air, so that it is easy to inhale for breathing; and the upward direction of the flame of fire, for if it were like water, flaming to the right and left, fires would multiply. As for air, it does not accept burning.

As for His words (khalaqahu, "He created it"), Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it in the past-tense form (fi'l al-madi), taking the clause as a qualifier of "thing" (shay'), meaning every one of the existing things that He created, and of which they know much.

The rest read it with a sukun on the lam (khalqahu, as a noun), taking it as a noun that is a substitute of "everything" by comprehensive apposition (badal al-ishtimal).

[p. 216]

From this general description he moves to the creation of man, because the make-up of man contains subtleties in his outward and inward being, the greatest of which is the intellect.

"Man" (al-insan) is intended as a species. The beginning of his creation is the creation of his ancestor Adam, as in His words, ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels: prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 11], meaning: We created your father, then We fashioned him, then We said to the angels: prostrate to Adam. This meaning is indicated here by His words ﴿then He made his offspring from an extract﴾, for that began with the first offspring of Adam and Eve. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 10:

﴿And they say: "When we have become lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Nay, but they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord.﴾

The waw here is for the circumstantial (ḥāl), and the circumstance is for expressing wonder at them, how they deem the re-creation of creation impossible while they know the first origination. The re-creation is not more wondrous than the beginning of creation, especially the beginning of Adam's creation from non-existence. The absence of qad from the past-tense clause does not preclude its being a circumstantial clause in the strict sense.

The interrogative in "a'idhā ḍalalnā" is for wonder and denial of possibility; that is, they displayed in their speech the improbability of resurrection after the bodies have perished and mixed with the dust, as a deception of the believers and a promotion of their disbelief. Ḍalāl (losing one's way, being lost) means absence, and from it comes ḍalāl al-ṭarīq (losing the road), and al-ḍāllah (the lost animal), which has strayed far from its people so that its whereabouts are unknown. By this they meant: when the parts of our bodies are scattered within the earth and mixed with the earth's dust.

It has also been said: ḍalāl fī al-arḍ means entering into it, based on the usage "aḍalla al-nās al-mayyit," i.e., they buried the dead. They recited the verse of al-Nābigha in lamenting al-Nu'mān ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghassānī:

Then those who buried him returned with a clear sign, and there was left at al-Jawlān judgment and bounty.

Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī and Ya'qūb recited (﴿a'innā la-fī khalqin jadīdin﴾) with a single hamza, in the declarative form, being satisfied with the entry of the interrogative upon the first part of the clause and its complement. The rest recited (﴿a'innā la-fī khalqin jadīdin﴾) with two hamzas, the first for interrogation and the second as emphasis for the interrogative hamza entering upon "a'idhā ḍalalnā fī al-arḍ."
Ibn 'Āmir recited with the omission of the interrogative in both places, on the basis that the speech is a statement used in mockery (tahakkum).

The emphasis of the clause (﴿innā la-fī khalqin jadīdin﴾) with the particle "inna" is because they related the statement at which they wondered, which is what the Qur'an contains regarding the affirmation of the renewal of creation, so they related it in meaning, as in the other verse: ﴿And those who disbelieved said: "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you are completely disintegrated, you will be in a new creation?"﴾ [Saba': 7], that is, he will confirm that for you.

"Idhā" is an adverbial time expression, and it is governed by the meaning of existence (al-kawn) contained in the clause (﴿innā la-fī khalqin jadīdin﴾). Khalq is a verbal noun.

"Fī" is for figurative containment, and its meaning is accompaniment.

Jadīd means newly made, that is, other than our former creation in which we were.

"Bal" in ﴿Nay, but they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ is a turning away from their speech; that is, their denial of resurrection is not due to considering it improbable or impossible, because the proofs of its possibility are clear to everyone who reflects. Rather, the motive for their denial of it is their disbelief in the meeting with God, that is, their disbelief which they received from their leaders without any proof. The meaning is: rather, they have already become certain of the absence of resurrection, so they are obstinate in disbelief and persist in it, and signs and proofs do not benefit them. Thus the disbelief affirmed here is a specific disbelief, different from the disbelief indicated by their saying (﴿a'idhā ḍalalnā fī al-arḍ, innā la-fī khalqin jadīdin﴾), for that is disbelief in the meeting with God, but they manifested it in the form of improbability, to sow doubt among the believers and promote their disbelief.

The placement of the prepositional phrase before "kāfirūn" is for the sake of maintaining the rhyme (ri'āyah 'alā al-fāṣilah). The use of the nominal clause conveys the continuity of their disbelief and their steadfastness in it.

[Page 220]

﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned.﴾

This is a resumptive new sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a sentence beginning a new topic), following the manner of relating speeches (*hikayat al-muqawalat*). The sentence "Say" (*qul*) carries the sense of a reply to their statement: ﴿When we have strayed into the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ (al-Sajdah: 10). The Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, was commanded to restate to them that they will be resurrected after death. The purpose of the sentence is therefore His saying ﴿then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 15), since it is the focus of their denial. As for the statement that the Angel of Death takes them, it is mentioned to remind them of death, which they do not deny. However, the life of this world has diverted them from considering the possibility of resurrection and preparing for it, so they were reminded of it. Then the mention of the Angel of Death was incorporated into it, to intensify fear of death and to allude to a warning through His saying ﴿who has been entrusted with you﴾, for he is entrusted with every dead person, to treat them according to what befits them at the seizing of their souls.

In this there is a refutation of their ignorance, namely that death is in the hand of Allah, the Exalted, and that just as He created them He causes them to die, and just as He causes them to die He gives them life again, and that causing death and giving life are by His permission and by His subjugation of His angels in both states. This is a refutation of their saying ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 24). So Allah informed them that they do not escape from the grip of His control even for the blink of an eye, neither in the state of life nor in the state of death. And if their death occurs through the act of the Angel of Death, who has been entrusted by Allah with seizing their souls, it becomes clear that their souls will be returned to them whenever Allah wills.

*Al-tawaffi* means causing death. It has been discussed in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿It is He who takes you by night﴾ (al-An'am: 60) in Surat al-An'am, and in His saying ﴿If you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve﴾ (al-Anfal: 50) in al-Anfal.

*Malak al-mawt* (the Angel of Death) is the angel entrusted with seizing souls. He is mentioned in the Qur'an in the singular, as here, and in the plural in His saying ﴿If you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve﴾ (al-Anfal: 50) in Surat al-Anfal, and His saying ﴿Our messengers take him* (al-An'am: 61) in Surat al-An'am. That is because Allah made many angels for seizing souls, and made the one who conveys Allah's command concerning this 'Izra'il. Thus ascribing the taking (*tawaffi*) to him is like ascribing it to Allah in His saying ﴿Allah takes the souls﴾ (al-Zumar: 42). He made the angels entrusted with seizing souls his assistants, and they hand the souls over to 'Izra'il, and he seizes them and deposits them in the abodes that Allah has prepared for them,

and the name 'Izra'il is not mentioned in the Qur'an. It has also been said that *malak al-mawt* in this verse is intended as a collective noun (*jins*), so it is like His saying ﴿Our messengers take him﴾ (al-An'am: 61).

﴿If only you could see when the criminals will hang their heads before their Lord, saying: "Our Lord, we have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will act righteously. Indeed, we are now certain."﴾

He follows the mention of their denial of resurrection by depicting the condition of those who deny it at the moment it takes effect, which is when they are gathered for the reckoning. In describing their condition he uses the method of omitting the answer to *law* (*lau*, "if"). This omission serves the same purpose as the answer itself: the listener's mind goes in every direction in picturing the awfulness of their state and the terror of their standing before their Lord. He also addresses the speech to an unspecified listener, to show that their condition has reached such a degree of clarity that it is not restricted to any particular addressee. The meaning is: "If only you could see, O observer, you would see a tremendous matter."

"The criminals" (*al-mujrimun*) are those who said (﴿When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we really be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]). The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is an instance of *iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār* (stating the noun where a pronoun would be expected), intended to record against them that in this statement they are criminals, that is, they are committing a crime, namely the crime of denying the Messenger (ﷺ) and nullifying the evidence.

*Al-nākis* is the one who makes the highest part of a thing the lowest. It is said: *nakkasa ra'sahu*, "he lowered his head," because he is like one who has turned the top of a thing downward.

Lowering the heads is a sign of humiliation and remorse, which they encounter through rebuke and disgrace.

*Al-'indiyyah* ("being with") here is the "being with" of authority: they are under the judgment of their Lord and cannot find any way to evade it. This is likened to being in a place specific to their Lord, in that they cannot escape from Him.

The clause ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾ and what follows is a quoted speech of an omitted verb of saying, which the context indicates. It stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "hanging their heads, saying" or "as those who say: we have seen and heard." They say this out of remorse and in acknowledgment that what the Qur'an threatened them with is true.

The objects of "we have seen" and "we have heard" are omitted because the context makes them clear. The meaning is: we saw, from the evident signs, what confirms what He told us; they saw the resurrection from the graves and saw how those who denied were treated. And we heard, from the words of the angels, what confirms the threat with which we were threatened. Thus we came to know that what the Messenger (ﷺ) called us to is the truth, by which salvation from the punishment is attained. "So send us back" to the world, "and we will act righteously," as they said in another place: ﴿Our Lord, delay us to a near term, and we will answer Your call and follow the messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 44].

His saying ﴿indeed, we are certain﴾ gives the reason for the fulfilment of the promise to act righteously: they have become certain of the truth of what the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them to. Thus *inna* here takes the place of the connecting *fa'* (of consequence), which conveys causation. The meaning is: nothing prevents us from fulfilling what we were promised except doubt or denial; we now know with certainty that what we were called to is the truth.

The active participle in His saying *mūqinūn* ("certain") refers to the present time, as is its original function.

This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) placed between the words ascribed to the speakers, understood as "Our Lord, we have seen and heard" [32:12], and the response to it, "So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting" [32:14]. The wāw at the beginning of the sentence is an interjectional wāw, and it is of the type of the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl).

The object of the verb of will is omitted, as is usual for the verb of will when it occurs as a conditional, since the object is understood from what the answer of the condition indicates.

The meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have compelled every soul to be guided by nature, without choice, just as the animals were made to follow what they were inspired to in the order of life for their kinds. The souls would then have had no need to reflect on guidance and its opposite, nor for a summons from God to the path of guidance. But when God willed to entrust the human species with the cultivation of this world, to make it a sign of His knowledge and wisdom, and to prefer it over all the species and kinds that populate this world, this wisdom required that He create in the human a mind (ʿaql) by which he perceives benefit and harm, perfection and deficiency, righteousness and corruption, building and destruction. Through reflection, the consequences of actions that are ambiguous and disguised are revealed to him, so that he has the choice of what proceeds from him among the kinds and types of acts that are within his power, by a will directed toward one thing or its opposite. He also created in him, from the means and instruments of action, the limbs and organs, when they are sound. Thus he is able to act or not to act in accordance with his inclination, his choice, and his acquisition (kasb)." This meaning is what al-Ash'arī called acquisition (kasb) and capacity (istiṭāʿa). God undertook to assist him in what He created for him of perception, calling him to what God wants from him of guidance and righteousness in this world, through messengers of his own kind who convey to him the will of their Lord. He made them of angelic qualities and made them intermediaries between Him and people in conveying the will of their Lord to them.

His promise to people of recompense for doing good and doing evil, with what contains an incitement to good and a deterrent from evil, is also part of this.

God willed to honor this kind by making from it inhabitants of the eternal realm of perfection, the realm of spiritual realities. So He placed for the people of religious perfection lofty ranks, varying in the eternal abode according to the variation of their souls in the field of racing toward perfections. And He made the opposites of these people inhabitants of the abyss of deficiencies, so He filled that abyss, called Jahannam, with them.

This is the meaning of His words: "But the word from Me has come into effect: I will fill Hell with jinn and humankind, all together" [32:13]. It attains a level of conciseness that reaches the level of inimitability, since it omits most of what is meant by the adversative particle (ḥarf al-istidrāk) that follows His words, "Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance" [32:13]. The implication of the adversative is that it should be understood as: "But We did not will that; rather, We willed to create people free to choose between the two paths of guidance and error, and We placed in them motives of hope and fear, and showed them the means of salvation and entanglement with the laws." He said, may He be exalted: "And We showed him the two highways" [90:10], that is, the two paths. And We confirmed the reports about the two recompenses, the promise and the threat, with Paradise and Hell. So Hell will indeed be filled with the people of error from the jinn and humankind, all together. This is included in His words, "the word from Me has come into effect: I will fill Hell with jinn and humankind, all together," by something resembling the implication necessitated by the text (dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ). The Prophet ﷺ alluded to this when he said: "God created Paradise and created for it its fillers, and He created the Fire and created for it its fillers."

The restriction in the explicit statement to the indication of the omitted part, the fate of the people of error, was chosen because it is more suitable to the context of the interjection following the speech of the people of error on the Day of Recompense, and because it is more evident in linking the content of the interjected clause with the content of their request. That is: if their being returned to the world so that they might do righteous deeds were required by Our wisdom, We would have made them inclined to guidance in their worldly life, and they would have done righteous deeds by compulsion and coercion.

So the intended meaning of "the word" is what God threatened to the people of polytheism and error.

Al-Jinnah: the jinn, who are devils.

Most of the exegetes made His words, "Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance," through to the end, a reply directed from God, may He be exalted, to the guilty ones concerning their saying, "Our Lord, we have seen" [32:12], and so on.

The presence of the wāw at the beginning of this utterance indicates that it is not a reply to the polytheists' statement on that day. They are less deserving than to be made recipients of this wisdom. Rather, their due is to be turned away from in reply to them, as occurs in the verses of Surat al-Mu'minun: "They will say: Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people" [23:106]. "Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we are indeed wrongdoers" [23:107]. "He will say: Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me" [23:108]. Also because it does not meet their question, for they asked to be returned so that they might do righteous deeds. Their speech was not an excuse for their error, claiming that God did not give them guidance in the worldly life. Rather, this is an explanation from God brought for the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, so that they may comprehend the subtleties of divine wisdom.

He departed from the idafa construction in "the word from Me" [ḥaqqa al-qawlu minnī], so He did not say "the word of Me" [ḥaqqa qawlī], because the intention was to point to a known statement, which is what is in Surat Sad: "I will surely fill Hell with you and whoever follows you among them, all together" [38:85]. That is, the known word has come into effect. The initial min (minna al-ibtidāʾiyya) was brought in to magnify the matter of this statement, in that it is from God.

He turned away from the pronoun of majesty to the pronoun of the self (nafs) to indicate exclusive authority in disposing of the matter, and because it is the original form, along with the variation this difference provides in style.

This is a response to their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12], which is an acknowledgment of the truth of what they used to deny, and their saying ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12] indicates it. So the *fa'* (ف) is for deriving a response (*tafri' jawab*) from their acknowledgment, as a form of argumentation against them, in accordance with the implication of their own acknowledgment. That is, it follows from your acknowledgment of the truth of what the Messenger was calling you to, that the punishment of the Fire will befall you.

[Page 226]

The use of a derivative *fa'* by the speaker upon what is the speech of the addressee is a binding of them with the proof, like the *fa'*s in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are expelled"﴾ [al-Hijr: 34], and His saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the day they are resurrected"﴾ [al-Hijr: 36], ﴿He said, "Then indeed you are among those reprieved"﴾ [al-Hijr: 37], ﴿until the day of the appointed time﴾ [al-Hijr: 38], ﴿He said, "Then by Your might, I will surely mislead them all"﴾ [Sad: 82], and His saying ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say﴾ [Sad: 84], ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together"﴾ [Sad: 85]. These are five *fa'*s, each of which is a derivation by the speaker upon the speech of another. This has already been discussed under conjunction by *wa'* at His saying, "And of my descendants" [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The use of *dhawq* (tasting) to mean general perception is a *majaz mursal* (metonymy based on a non-analogical relation), which was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The object of *dhuqu* (taste) is omitted, indicated by the context, that is: "So taste what you are in of that which called you to ask to return to the world."

The first *nisyan* (forgetting) means neglect and squandering. It was discussed at His saying: "and he forgot" in Surat Ta-Ha.

The *ba'* is causal, that is, because of your neglect of preparing for this day. The *nisyan* in His saying ﴿"We have forgotten you"﴾ is used to mean deprivation of honour, through *mushakala* (figure of correspondence, where a word is used because of its counterpart in the same sentence).

*Liqa'* (meeting): its literal meaning is coming upon a thing. From it comes the meeting of a man with another, and from it comes *mula>qat* (encounter). And from it: a person's finding of a lost thing or the like. It has also come as *shay' laqan*, meaning something cast aside. The *liqa'* of the day in this verse is a figurative usage for the day's arrival and existence unexpectedly, as if it had been come upon.

The attribution of "day" to the pronoun of the addressees is mockery of them, because they used to deny it. When they realized it, it was made as though it were especially theirs, by way of a sarcastic metaphor (*isti'arah tahakkumiyyah*), because when a day is attributed to a people or a group, if it is a day of their victory over their enemy, the poet al-Samaw'al said:

*And our days are renowned against our enemy, with known marks and known white blazes.*

[Page 227]

And they say: "The days of such-and-such a clan over such-and-such a clan," meaning the days of their victory. The reason for this is that the estimated sense of the attribution is with the *lam* (of possession), and it conveys the specific connection derived from ownership. Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*And days of ours, bright and long.*

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the true day﴾ [al-Naba': 39], meaning the day of the victory of the believers over the polytheists in the Hereafter, a victory that is everlasting, that is, not like your days in the world, which are days of fleeting victory.

The indication by "this" (*hadha*) to the day is for magnifying it.

The clause ﴿"Indeed We have forgotten you"﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), because when the guilty ones heard what they knew from His saying ﴿So taste for what you forgot of the meeting of this your day﴾, they became eager to know the extent of this punishment that is tasted, and whether there is any escape for them from it, and whether they would be granted what they asked of returning to the world so that they might make up what they had missed of belief. So they were informed that God delays their matter, that is, He does not respond to them. This is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for abandoning them in what they have been made to taste. His saying was already mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿He said, "Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them, and likewise today you are forgotten"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126]. So the forgetting is compared to it, to show justice in the recompense, and that it is of the same kind as the deed for which one is recompensed.

This news has been confirmed by emphatic elements: the particle of emphasis, and the presenting of the statement in the past tense form contrary to what the apparent sense requires (the present tense), to convey that the action is so certain that it is as though it has already happened and occurred.

His saying ﴿And taste the punishment of the eternal abode for what you used to do﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) upon ﴿So taste for what you forgot﴾. Although it conveys the emphasis of the imposition of punishment upon them, its coordination takes into account the difference between the two clauses in their objects and restrictions, a difference that requires that the second clause be considered as conveying a different benefit. The first clause includes that among the cause of their deserving that tasting is their neglect of reflecting upon the arrival of this day, and the second clause includes that this punishment is continuous, and that the cause of the continuation of the punishment and its not being lightened is their wrong deeds, which are more general than their forgetting of the meeting of that day.

[Page 227]

This is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*, a new sentence) arising from His saying, "Or do they say, 'He has invented it?'" (al-Sajdah: 3). The context became free for it after the rebuke and threat directed at the disbelievers for their disbelief in meeting Allah. The nominal form of the sentence ﴿Nay, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10] indicates that they are steadfast in disbelief in the meeting with Allah and persistent in it. This is among the things the verses of the Qur'an warned them of. Denying the meeting with Allah is therefore denying what the Qur'an brought. Thus they do not believe, and only those who have the qualities described here believe in the verses of Allah.

The "verses" here means the verses of the Qur'an, as indicated by His saying "﴿who, when they are reminded of them﴾", with the *kaf* pronounced with a shadda, meaning that their remembrance is repeated to them and their recitation is repeated to their hearing.

The particle *innama* ("only") indicates a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), meaning: those who believe in the verses of Allah are those who, when they are reminded of them, reminding them of what they had already heard, do not hesitate to show submission to Allah, unlike those who said (﴿"When we have become lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]). This is a discouragement for the Prophet ﷺ regarding their faith, and an allusion to them that their belief will not benefit the Muslims, nor will they anger them by their obstinacy in disbelief.

The present tense form *yu'minu* ("believes") is chosen because of what it conveys: that they continually renew their faith and grow in certainty from time to time, as was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surat al-Baqarah. Otherwise, the believers had already attained their faith in the past, and the past tense would be more common in describing their state in ordinary speech, were it not for this particular feature. For this reason they are identified by the relative pronoun and its clause, whose meaning indicates that they are firmly established in faith. The conveying of the verses of the Qur'an to them and their recitation to their ears is expressed by "reminding" (*tadhkir*), which implies that what the verses contain are established truths in their minds. They do not impart to them any new benefit that was not already present in their souls, but they add to them reminder, ﴿for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 55]. This quality contained in the relative clause is their state, by which they are known because of the strength of their faith, and by which they are distinguished from those who disbelieved. It does not require that those who did not prostrate upon hearing the verses and did not glorify their Lord with His praise are not among the believers. Rather, this is the state of the perfection of faith, and it is the state of the believers with the Prophet ﷺ on that day, by which they were known. This is like when you say to someone asking about the scholars of a town: "They are those who wear turbans of such and such a description." It is reported in the biography of Malik ibn Anas that he did not issue legal opinions until seventy men wearing a *muhannak* (a turban wrapped under the chin) gave him permission, meaning scholars who place a piece of their turban under their chin, which was the dress of the people of jurisprudence and hadith. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I said to my mother, 'Let me go and write down knowledge.' She said, 'Come and dress in the clothes of knowledge.' So she dressed me in folded garments, placed the *tawilah* (a tall cap) on my head, and wrapped a turban over it."

*Al-kharur* is falling from a height to a lower place.

*As-sujud* is placing the forehead on the ground, intending glorification and submission.

*Sujjadan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) clarifying the purpose of *kharru*, meaning: prostrating to Allah and thanking Him for what He bestowed upon them of knowledge and faith, as indicated by its being joined with His saying: ﴿and they glorify the praise of their Lord﴾. The *ba'* in it indicates accompaniment (*mulabasah*). It was mentioned in Surat al-Isra': ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their faces in prostration﴾ [al-Isra': 107].

The conditional sentence indicates the continuous connection between the occurrence of the response and the occurrence of the condition, and their inseparability.

The negation of arrogance from them is expressed by a verbal predicate to indicate that this quality is specific to them, meaning in contrast to the polytheists, whose character was arrogance. They do not accept for themselves submission to a prophet from among themselves, and they said: ﴿"Why were the angels not sent down upon us, or do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

His saying ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾ is the place of a prostration among the prostrations of Qur'anic recitation, in hope that the reciter will be one of those whom Allah praised, saying that when they are reminded of the verses of Allah, they prostrate. Thus the reciter follows their example.

The clause ﴿their sides forsake their beds﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the relative pronoun, meaning: those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down, and of their state is ﴿their sides forsake their beds﴾. Alternatively, it is a resumptive statement.

The present tense is used in it to indicate that this occurs repeatedly and continually from them during many of the times set aside for lying down, which are the times when sleep is normally taken.

*At-tajafi* is distancing and abandoning. The meaning is that the withdrawal of their sides from their beds recurs during a single night, meaning they frequently stay awake in night prayer and supplication to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ explained it as a man's prayer in the middle of the night, as will come in the hadith of Mu'adh in al-Tirmidhi.

*Al-madaji'* are the bedding, plural of *madja'*, which is the place of lying down, meaning reclining for rest and sleep. The *al-* in it is a substitute for the possessive pronoun, meaning "their beds," as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 41].

This is an allusion to the polytheists, who spend their nights in sleep, which does not keep them from reflection, but they fall down as cattle fall. 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah clearly expressed this meaning in his saying, describing the Prophet ﷺ, who was the master of those concerned with this matter:

*He spends the night, his side withdrawing from his bed, when the beds weigh heavily upon the polytheists.*

The clause ﴿they call upon their Lord﴾ may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of their sides, but it is best to make it a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿their sides forsake their beds﴾.

*Khawfan wa tama'an* ("in fear and in hope") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, interpreted as "fearful and hopeful," meaning: out of fear of His anger, and in hope of His good pleasure and reward. In other words, these are two qualities of theirs.

They may also be in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlih*), meaning: for the sake of fear of their Lord and hope for His mercy.

When He mentioned their preference for drawing near to Allah over the pleasures of their bodies, He also mentioned their preference for Him over what brings them the enjoyment of other pleasures, namely wealth, as they spend from it what, if they had kept it, would have been a source of comfort for them. So He said: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾, meaning they give charity from it, even if the wealthy among them are less well off than the poor.

Then Allah magnified their reward when He said: ﴿So no soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾, meaning no soul among the people of this world can reach knowledge of what Allah has prepared for them. The Prophet ﷺ said: Allah the Exalted said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." This shows that the intended meaning of "soul" (*nafs*) in this verse is the people of human souls, because the perceptions of the intellect end at what the eyes perceive of visible things, of beauty and adornment, and what the ears perceive of fine speech, praiseworthy words, and sweet melodies, and at what the imagination reaches of forms that the mind constructs from a combination of what it has known of visible and audible things, such as rivers of honey, wine, or milk, palaces and domes of pearls, trees of emerald, flowers of ruby, and soil of musk and ambergris. All of that is little compared to what has been prepared for them in Paradise of these described things, and the descriptions of describers cannot reach it, because the limit of description is confined to what the signifying power of languages reaches of what can occur to human hearts. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "and no human heart has conceived." This is like their saying, when glorifying something: "No one knows this except Allah."

The poet said:

*None knows what stirred us, except Allah, on the evening of the abodes' mounds and their *Shama* (a place name).*

He expressed those blessings as "what has been concealed" because they are hidden and cannot be perceived except in the world of eternity.

*Qurrat al-a'yun* ("comfort of the eyes") is a metaphor for joy, as was mentioned previously in His saying "and be comforted (*wa qarri 'ayna*)" in Surat Maryam.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *ukhfiya* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, in the past tense of the passive voice.

Hamzah and Ya'qub read *ukhfi* in the present tense beginning with the *hamzah* of the first person and with the *ya'* quiescent. *Jaza'an* ("as a reward") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state from *ma ukhfiya lahum*. The Prophet ﷺ explained that it is a reward for these righteous deeds in a *gharib* (rare) hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, inform me of a deed that will admit me into Paradise and keep me far from the Fire.' He said: 'You have asked about something great, and it is indeed easy for those whom Allah makes it easy for: worship Allah, associate nothing with Him, establish prayer, pay zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform Hajj to the House.' Then he said: 'Shall I not direct you to the gates of good? Fasting is a shield, charity extinguishes sins as water extinguishes fire, and a man's prayer in the middle of the night.' Then he recited: ﴿their sides forsake their beds﴾ until he reached ﴿...they used to do﴾..." the hadith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verses 18–20:

[Page 231]
﴿Is then he who is a believer like one who is a defiant sinner? They are not equal.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the gardens of refuge as a lodging, for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿But as for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire. Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾

This is linked with the fa' (fa') to what preceded of the promise to the believers and the threat to the disbelievers. The interrogative with the hamza (hamza of interrogation) is used to express denial of equality between the believer and the disbeliever. It is a denial that treats the listener as one who is amazed at the gulf between the recompense of the two groups on that Day, so the denial is directed at that amazement, in the sense of a rhetorical resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani).

The kaf (kaf) is for comparison in the recompense.

The clause ﴿lā yastawūn﴾ (they are not equal) is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) to the intended meaning of the interrogation.

The fasiq (defiant sinner) here is: one who is not a believer, by the indication of His saying after it: ﴿It will be said to them: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ So the intended meaning is: defiance from faith, which is shirk, and this is a very common usage in the Qur'an.

Then He emphasized both recompenses by mentioning a synonym of their meaning with an added benefit. So the clause ﴿fa-lahum jannatu al-ma'wa﴾ to its end emphasizes the content of the clause ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them﴾ [al-Sajda: 17] to its end.

And the clause ﴿fa-ma'wahumu al-nar﴾ to its end emphasizes the content of the clause ﴿So taste (it) because you forgot the meeting of this your Day﴾ [al-Sajda: 14] up to ﴿what you used to do﴾ [al-Sajda: 14].

The relative pronoun man (man) in both places is general, by the indication of the detail in the plural in His saying ﴿As for those who believed﴾ etc. and ﴿As for those who defied﴾, so the verse was not revealed concerning a specific individual, as has been said.

Al-ma'wa (refuge): the place to which one resorts, i.e., one returns to it.

The definite article in it is for previous reference (al-'ahd), i.e., the refuge of the believers, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Near it is the garden of refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15]. You may also take the article as a substitute for the genitive complement, i.e., their refuge, by the indication of His saying in contrast with ﴿fa-ma'wahumu al-nar﴾.

The idafa of jannat (gardens) to al-ma'wa is an idafa of the qualified to the qualifier, for the purpose of lightening the expression, and it occurs in speech even though the Basrans and Kufans have disagreed about its interpretation, a disagreement without benefit. This is like their saying: masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque), and His saying, exalted: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], and their saying: 'isha' al-akhira (the last night prayer). The meaning is: "So for them are the gardens of refuge," i.e., those promised them.

Nuzulan (as a lodging) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from jannat al-ma'wa. Nuzul, with two dammas, is derived from nuzul (descending), and it is applied to what is prepared for the guest of provision and hospitality. In al-Kashshaf it is said: "Nuzul: the gift of the one who descends," then it became general, i.e., it is applied to a gift even without hospitality, as a metonymy by extension (majaz mursal). I say: it is also applied to the place where a guest alights, and for the sake of these applications the exegetes differ regarding its intended meaning in some verses, observing what suits the context of the speech.

Al-Zajjaj explained it in this verse and similar ones as "the dwelling place," and he explained it in His saying, exalted: ﴿Is that better as a lodging, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ [al-Saffat: 62], saying: He says: "Is that better in the category of lodgings in which one can remain, or the lodging of the people of the Fire?" This was mentioned at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

The ba' in ﴿bima kanu ya'malun﴾ (for what they used to do) is causal (sababiyya).

His saying ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ has a parallel that was mentioned in Surat al-Hajj.

This question was raised by Ibn al-Hajib in his Amali, and he answered with two aspects. The second: the sentence is a report of what will be said to them on that Day, so it is appropriate to report it as it was said to them, and there was no prior mention of the Fire in what is said to them.

Then He emphasized both recompenses by mentioning a synonym of their meaning with an added benefit. So the clause ﴿fa-lahum jannatu al-ma'wa﴾ to its end emphasizes the content of the clause ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them﴾ [al-Sajda: 17] to its end.

And the clause ﴿fa-ma'wahumu al-nar﴾ to its end emphasizes the content of the clause ﴿So taste (it) because you forgot the meeting of this your Day﴾ [al-Sajda: 14] up to ﴿what you used to do﴾ [al-Sajda: 14].

The relative pronoun man (man) in both places is general, by the indication of the detail in the plural in His saying ﴿As for those who believed﴾ etc. and ﴿As for those who defied﴾, so the verse was not revealed concerning a specific individual, as has been said.

Al-ma'wa (refuge): the place to which one resorts, i.e., one returns to it.

The definite article in it is for previous reference (al-'ahd), i.e., the refuge of the believers, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Near it is the garden of refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15]. You may also take the article as a substitute for the genitive complement, i.e., their refuge, by the indication of His saying in contrast with ﴿fa-ma'wahumu al-nar﴾.

The idafa of jannat (gardens) to al-ma'wa is an idafa of the qualified to the qualifier, for the purpose of lightening the expression, and it occurs in speech even though the Basrans and Kufans have disagreed about its interpretation, a disagreement without benefit. This is like their saying: masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque), and His saying, exalted: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], and their saying: 'isha' al-akhira (the last night prayer). The meaning is: "So for them are the gardens of refuge," i.e., those promised them.

Nuzulan (as a lodging) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from jannat al-ma'wa. Nuzul, with two dammas, is derived from nuzul (descending), and it is applied to what is prepared for the guest of provision and hospitality. In al-Kashshaf it is said: "Nuzul: the gift of the one who descends," then it became general, i.e., it is applied to a gift even without hospitality, as a metonymy by extension (majaz mursal). I say: it is also applied to the place where a guest alights, and for the sake of these applications the exegetes differ regarding its intended meaning in some verses, observing what suits the context of the speech.

Al-Zajjaj explained it in this verse and similar ones as "the dwelling place," and he explained it in His saying, exalted: ﴿Is that better as a lodging, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ [al-Saffat: 62], saying: He says: "Is that better in the category of lodgings in which one can remain, or the lodging of the people of the Fire?" This was mentioned at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

The ba' in ﴿bima kanu ya'malun﴾ (for what they used to do) is causal (sababiyya).

His saying ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ has a parallel that was mentioned in Surat al-Hajj.

It is appropriate in this verse to ask: why did He make the noun "the Fire" explicit in His saying "Taste the punishment of the Fire," although the noun "the Fire" had already been mentioned in His saying "fa-ma'wahumu al-nar"? The apparent requirement would have been the pronoun, by saying: "It will be said to them: Taste its punishment." This question was raised by Ibn al-Hajib in his Amali, and he answered with two aspects. The first: the context of the verse is threat, and in the explicit mention of the word "the Fire" there is a frightening effect that is absent in the pronoun. The second: the sentence is a report of what will be said to them on that Day, so it is appropriate to report it as it was said to them, and there was no prior mention of the Fire in what is said to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 21:

﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment, short of the greater punishment, so that perhaps they will return.﴾

This is a report that they will have another punishment, one that does not reach the extent of the Fire of the Hereafter, which they were promised.

Page 233
It is thus determined that the nearer punishment is the punishment of this world. The purpose of this is an allusion (ta'ridh) threatening them, since they hear this speech or it is conveyed to them. This is a warning of what befell them after the revelation of the verse, namely what they were afflicted with of hunger and fear, when they had been secure from both, and what befell them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture, and on the Day of the Conquest (Fath) of humiliation.

The clause ﴿so that perhaps they will return﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) concerning the wisdom of making them taste the nearer punishment in this world: that it is in hope of their return, that is, their return from disbelief to faith. What is meant is the return of those among them who are able to return, namely the living among them. The attribution of "return" to the pronoun of all of them is by way of considering the tribe and the group, that is, perhaps their group will return.

And so it was. Many people believed after the Day of Badr, and especially after the Conquest of Mecca. Thus those in whom the hoped-for return was realized became exempted from the generality of "those who defied" (alladhina fasaqu) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿But as for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire; whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20], and so that threat remained for those who died in polytheism, which is the question of muwafah (dying in a state of faith or disbelief) according to al-Ash'ari.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 32, verse 22:**

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals.﴾

This is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) with the sentence ﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them...﴾ [al-Sajdah: 15] to its end. It requires that those who said ﴿When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10] are not like those. So the discourse moves to report about them that they are the most unjust of people, because they are reminded of the signs of Allah when the Qur'an is recited to them, and they turn away from reflecting upon them and engage in idle talk about them. The signs of Allah here refer to the Qur'an.

The use of the particle **thumma** ("then") in the conjunction of the clause *aʿraḍa* ("turned away") indicates the remoteness of the rank of turning away from the signs after being reminded of them. It expresses astonishment and wonder at their condition, as in the verse of Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlbah al-Ḥārithī:

*None removes the distress except the son of a free woman,*
*who sees the surges of death and then visits them.*

That is: it is astonishing that he advances into the places of destruction after witnessing the surges of death that overwhelm those who advanced into those places.

The **man** here is interrogative for denial (*istifhām inkārī*), as in His saying ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], meaning: there is no one more unjust than him. That is, no one is more unjust than him, because he wronged himself by depriving it of contemplation of what would benefit it; he wronged the signs by nullifying their benefit for some of those for whom benefit from them was intended; he wronged the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by denying him and turning away from him; and he wronged the right of his Lord, since he did not comply with what He willed from him.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾ is a resumptive explanatory sentence (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) arising from the magnification of the wrong of the one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord and turned away from them, because the listener anticipates the requital of that wrongdoer.

By "the criminals" is meant these wrongdoers. He turned away from mentioning them by pronoun in order to further record the enormity of their condition, that they are criminals in addition to being wrongdoers. It may be said that the criminals are more general than the wrongdoers, so their inclusion in the retribution against the criminals is a fortiori, and the sentence ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾ becomes a concluding sentence (*tadhyīl*).
