Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 23:

﴿Certainly We gave Moses the Book, so do not be in doubt about meeting him, and We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel.﴾

When the mention of the disbelievers' turning away from the signs of God, which are the signs of the Qur'an, came up in His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 22], there was a digression (istitrad) to console the Prophet (ﷺ). The consolation is that what he suffered from his people is the same as what Moses suffered from the people of Pharaoh, to whom he was sent. So the statement is used for consolation through comparison and analogy.

This sentence and what follows it, up to His words ﴿concerning which they used to differ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 25], are parenthetical insertions (i'tiradat). The emphasis by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of affirmation lies in what the statement is used for, which is consolation, not in the basic information itself, because that information does not need emphasis. By this, the elegance of the parenthetical insertion becomes clear, with the phrase ﴿so do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾ following on from the statement before it.

By His words ﴿We gave Moses the Book﴾ is meant: We sent Moses. Mentioning his being given the Book is a metonymy (kinayah) for his being sent, and the mention of the Book is embedded (idmaj) to honour Moses. It is not part of the comparison between the situation of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the situation of Moses (peace be upon him) in being denied by his people, because Moses was not denied by his people. Do you not see His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾, and so on? And so that the abundance of meanings in this verse can be achieved, which cannot be achieved without mentioning the Book.

The clause ﴿so do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, introduced by the fa' (of consequence), and this kind of insertion occurs frequently in speech, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿If he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 135] in the surah of al-Nisa'. It will also come at His words ﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid﴾ [Sad: 57] in the surah of Sad.

Al-mirya is doubt and hesitation. The particle of place (fi) is used figuratively (majaz) to express intense involvement, meaning: let doubt not surround you and take hold of you, i.e. do not be one who doubts that you will suffer what he suffered from his people.

The address may be to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the prohibition is used to request continuity in the absence of doubt. It is thus a prohibition whose purpose is to strengthen, like His words ﴿So do not be in doubt about what these people worship﴾ [Hud: 109], and it is not a request to bring about an abstention from doubt, since doubt had not occurred before.

Al-liqa' (meeting) is a verbal noun (ism masdar) of laqiya, and it is the more common usage, rather than liqan, which is the regular verbal noun. Al-liqa' is the encounter of the doer of this verb with its object, and it is used figuratively to mean reaching or befalling, as one says: "laqitu 'anā'an" (I met with hardship) and "laqitu 'araqa al-qirbah" (I met the sweat of the waterskin). Here it is figurative, meaning: do not be in doubt that what befell him will befall you. The pronoun of the third person refers to Moses. The word liqa' is a verbal noun added to its agent, meaning: that which Moses met from the people of Pharaoh of denial, i.e. the like of what Moses met. This omitted noun is indicated by the context, or the expression is taken as an intensive simile (tashbih baligh), like the saying "he is the full moon", meaning: a meeting like his meeting. This is then equivalent in meaning to many verses in the Qur'an that have this sense, such as His words, exalted is He: ﴿And messengers before you were denied, and they were patient at what they were denied and harmed, until Our help reached them﴾ [al-An'am: 34], and His words: (﴿And indeed they almost sought to drive you out of the land to expel you from it; and then they would not have remained after you except for a little﴾ [al-Isra': 76] ﴿as a practice concerning those We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra': 77]).

This is the best interpretation of the verse, and something close to it is transmitted from al-Hasan.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in "liqa'ihi" refers to Moses, in the sense: the like of what Moses met in his being sent, namely that the outcome of victory was his over the people of Pharaoh, and the attainment of guidance through the Book given to him, and its being supported by the guidance of the Children of Israel. In this case, this meaning is good news to the Prophet (ﷺ) that God will make this religion prevail.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in "liqa'ihi" refers to the Book, as in al-Kashshaf, but on the basis that the meaning is: so do not be in doubt about the meeting with the Book, i.e. about what you will encounter from being given the Book, which is the manner in which divine books are received, just as Moses received them. The prohibition is then used as a warning against one who thinks that he will not face in being given the Book the hardship that the messengers before him faced, namely from the harm and aversion of their people.

It is also permissible that the address in His words "so do not be" is not to a specific person, and is directed at those who doubted that the Qur'an was sent down from God, whether they were the polytheists or those from the People of the Book who instructed them, i.e. do not doubt that the Qur'an was sent down to a human being, for the Book was sent down to Moses, so do not be in doubt about the sending down of the Qur'an to Muhammad. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿When they said, "God has not sent down anything to a human being." Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as a light and guidance for the people?"﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. The prohibition is thus used in its literal sense, of requesting restraint from doubt about the sending down of the Qur'an. Interpreters have many other possibilities which do not yield a clear meaning, and among the most remote is taking the meeting in its literal sense, with the third-person pronoun referring to Moses, and that what is meant is his meeting [God] on the night of the Night Journey, which God promised him and fulfilled for him in this verse before it occurred. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Mubarrad said this when he tested Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj with this question.

The pronoun of the object in "wa ja'alnahu huda" may refer to the Book or to Moses, and both are a cause of guidance. So it is described as "guidance" for the sake of emphasis on the attainment of guidance through it. The phrase is coordinated with "We gave Moses the Book", and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. This is an allusion (ta'ridh) to the polytheists, since they did not give thanks for the blessing of God in that Muhammad was sent to them with the Qur'an so that they might be guided, but they turned away, and they were more deserving of eagerness to be guided by the Qur'an and by the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 24:

﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs.﴾

It is pointed out that this refers to the favour Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel when He made among them leaders guiding by the command of Allah. The "command" includes the revelation of the Shari'ah, since it is a command to it, and it includes taking up the position of guidance (irshad), for Allah commanded the scholars ('ulama') to make the Book clear (yubayyinu) and to guide to it. So when they guided, they guided by His command and by the knowledge that their prophets and their rabbis (ahbar) brought to them. Allah thus bestowed His blessing upon them through this when they were patient and were certain of what came to them from the Book of Allah and the miracles of their Messenger. If what is meant by His saying "they were certain of Our signs" is the proofs of the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him), then the meaning is: they were patient in the hardships of the obligations, and in the departure with them from the land of Egypt, and in what they encountered from Pharaoh and his people of torment and persecution, and in their wandering in the desert for forty years, and they reflected upon the signs and considered until they became certain.

And if what is meant by the signs is what is in the Torah of the legal rulings and admonitions, then calling them "signs" is an implied figurative correspondence (mushakalah taqdiriyyah) with what is common among the Muslims, namely calling the sentences of the Qur'an "signs" (ayat), because it is inimitable in its eloquence, beyond the capacity of human expression.

So they were indications of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is similar to what occurred in the hadith of the stoning of the two Jews, in the narrator's words: "the Jew placed his hand on the verse of stoning," i.e., the statement in the Torah that contains the ruling of stoning, and the narrator called it a "verse" by correspondence with the speech of the Qur'an.

In this there is an allusive glad tidings (ta'rid bil-bishara) to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they will be leaders of the religion of Islam and guides to the Muslims, since they were patient over what afflicted them for the sake of Allah from the harm of their people, and were patient over the hardships of the obligations and the enmity of their kin and people and their oppression of them.

The placing of "by Our signs" before "they are certain" is for the emphasis on the signs.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿lamma sabaru﴾ with a shaddah on the mim, and it is (lamma) which is a particle of existence for existence, called the temporal (tawqitiyyah), meaning: We made them leaders at the time when they were patient and were certain of Our signs.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a light mim, as being composed of the lam of causation and the verbal (masdariyyah) ma, meaning: We made them leaders because of their patience and their certainty.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, your Lord—He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani), because His saying, the Exalted: (﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24]) raises a question in the mind of the listener from among the believers, who heard what the Qur'an contains of the description of the disputes of the Children of Israel and their deviation from their religion. Many of them witnessed, in their own time, the Children of Israel not adorned with what befits the guidance their leaders had carried. So he wishes to know the cause of that. Thus in this verse is the answer to that, as instruction for the Prophet ﷺ and for the believers.

The address is to the Prophet, while the intended audience is his community, as a warning against that and an allusion to the obligation of avoiding disagreement that no valid call requires, concerning the interest of the community and the understanding of the religion.

Al-fasl (judgment): the deciding and ruling. It implies that their disagreement led them to nullify what guidance had come to them. So it is a disagreement not founded on evidence, nor running along the course of the basic principles of the Shari'ah; rather it is following desire and inclination toward the goods of this world, as the Qur'an described it in many verses in Surat al-Baqarah and elsewhere, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 105].

Not included in this is the disagreement of the leaders of the religion over the derivative rulings and over understanding the religion, which does not undermine its foundations nor contradict its texts. Rather, it is the application of its principles and its evidences to the circumstances suited to them, and the reconciliation of its apparently conflicting texts with one another. All of that is praiseworthy, not blameworthy. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ differed during his lifetime, and he did not rebuke anyone; and they differed after his death, and some of them did not rebuke others.

"That about which they used to differ" includes both the disagreement between the guided and the misguided among them, and the consensus of their whole community upon misguidance. For that is a contradiction between the consensus and what their shari'ah spoke and their prophets laid down. Among the greatest of that disagreement is their concealing the testimony to the mission of Muhammad ﷺ and their denial of the covenant taken from them through their prophets.

The pronoun "huwa" in His saying "huwa yafsilu" is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), restricting the judging to Him, the Exalted, as an allusion that what the Qur'an mentions of some of what they disputed against their prophets is not hoped to make them refrain from their disagreement; rather it is for the recording against them and cutting off their excuse, because they do not accept proof. So judgment between them will not take place except on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 26:

﴿Has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them, through whose dwellings they walk? Indeed, in that are signs. Will they not then listen?﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 22]. Since that reminder was continuous, like His saying ﴿And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Rather, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], the guidance (al-hady), meaning the knowledge sought through this interrogative, encompassed guidance to the proof of resurrection and to the proof of punishment for turning away from the reminder. So His saying ﴿how many generations We destroyed before them﴾ conveys two meanings:

First: the destruction of nations who were before them, after which these polytheists came. This is an illustration (tamthil) of resurrection and an bringing near of its possibility.

Second: the destruction of nations who denied their messengers, so there is a lesson (ʿibrah) for them that there may befall them the like of what befell those.

The interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari), meaning: they have not been guided by the proofs of reflection and reasoning that the Qur'an brought them, so they turned away from them, and they have not taken admonition from the fates (masarii) of the nations who denied their prophets. In their destruction are signs that deter their like from following what they followed.

The pronoun in ﴿لهم﴾ refers either to the criminals (al-mujrimun) or to the one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord. "Yahdi" is from al-hidayah (guidance), which is indication and direction; it is said: "hadahu ila kadha" (he guided him to such-and-such).

The verb yahdi is here construed with the meaning of yubayyinu (makes clear), so it takes the preposition lam, conveying clear and manifest guidance. A parallel to it has preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 100] in Surat al-A'raf. The verb of guidance was chosen in this verse to intend an indication that encompasses both observation and hearing the reports of those nations, as a preparation for His saying at its end ﴿Will they not then listen?﴾, and because the abundance (kathrah) derived from the relative kam (kam al-khabariyyah) is only obtained through arranging the inference across successive reports, and is not obtained all at once as the indication of direct observations is obtained.

The agent (fa'il) of yahdi is what the relative kam indicates of the meaning of abundance. It is not permitted, according to the majority (al-jumhur), to make kam the agent of yahdi, because kam al-khabariyyah is a noun that has priority of position in usage (lahu al-sadarah fi al-isti'mal), since its origin is interrogative, so it has been extended in its use.

It is permissible to make kam the agent according to those who do not stipulate that kam al-khabariyyah must be at the head of the sentence. In al-Kashshaf it is allowed that the agent is the clause "how many We destroyed," in the sense of quoting this saying, as one says: "La ilaha illa Allah" protects blood and property, meaning this utterance, that is, the pronouncing of it, for adopting Islam.

It is also permissible that the agent be the pronoun of the Majesty (Allah), indicated by the context, meaning: "Has Allah not made clear to them? For Allah has explained that to them and reminded them of the fates of the deniers." In this case the clause "how many We destroyed" is a resumption (istinaf).

"Has it not seen how many generations We destroyed before them" [al-An'am: 6] has preceded at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

The inference here is attached to the abundance conveyed by kam al-khabariyyah, because the repetition of the occurrence of generations and their passing away is a stronger indication than observing the traces of a single nation.

﴿Through whose dwellings they walk﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "awa lam yarawa" (have they not seen), and the meaning is: they pass by the places in which remain traces of their dwellings, such as the rock of Thamud and the abodes of Madyan, so the observation of their dwellings supports the reports conveyed about their annihilation. These are indications of the possibility of resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60] ﴿in that We replace your likes and create you in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61], and indications of what befalls those who deny the messengers; in every nation and place there are many indications, some similar and some different.

Since what is transmitted of the reports of those nations, the changes of their conditions, the passing of their strength and their comfort, is more forceful as an indication and admonition to the polytheists, His saying ﴿Will they not then listen?﴾ is appended to it as a rhetorical interrogative (istifham taqriri) mixed with reproach, because bringing the present tense "yasma'una" (they hear) indicates that hearing the reports of those nations is repeated and renewed, so the reproach upon the affirmation sought through the interrogative is more fitting, unlike what follows it, His saying ﴿Will they not then see?﴾. The rhetorical interrogative directed at a negated statement has been common, and it has preceded at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130] in Surat al-An'am, and at His saying ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them?﴾ [al-A'raf: 148] in Surat al-A'raf.

صفحة ٢٤١

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 32, verse 27:

﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops of which their livestock and they themselves eat? Will they not then see?﴾

It is coordinated with (ʿaṭf) the preceding "Or have they not been guided..." (awa lam yahdi lahum). The argument is attached here to sight (al-ru'yah) because the revival of the land after its death, and then the bringing forth of vegetation from it, is an evident (mushāhadah) proof. The present tense in His words "nasūqu" (We drive) was chosen to evoke (istiḥḍār) the wondrous scene that points to the overwhelming power.

Al-sawq (driving) is: urging something on from behind.

Al-mā' (the water) is rainwater, and its driving to the land is the driving of the clouds, which carry it by the winds that move the clouds from one atmosphere to another; thus the condition of the winds and clouds is likened to the condition of one who drives a beast. The definite article in "al-ard" (the land) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins).

Al-juruz (the barren land) is a noun for the land whose vegetation has been cut off. It is derived from al-jarz, which is the cutting off of plants and herbage, either due to the dryness of the land or to grazing; al-jarz means cutting. The cutting sword is called jurāz. A rajaz poet said, describing the teeth of a she-camel:

"She strikes on thorns with a cut, chopped (juraz miqdab), and she grinds the old (fodder) grinding it, a wonder."

So al-ard al-juruz is the land whose vegetation has been cut off. The land that does not produce plants, such as salt flats (sibakh), is not called juruz. Al-zar' (crops) is what grows through the sowing of its seeds in the land, such as barley, wheat and clover (al-fiṣfiṣah). The eating of livestock is mostly from pasture (kala'), not from crops; so the mention of crops by name, followed by the mention of livestock eating, indicates an implied term, namely "and pasture" (wa kala'). Thus there is ellipsis (iktifa') in the speech. The intended meaning is: "and bring forth thereby crops and pasture, of which their livestock and they themselves eat."

Purposes of this surah

Many of the verses of this surah have occasions of revelation, and most of it was revealed to refute the hypocrites, who uttered statements intending to harm the Prophet (ﷺ).

The most important of its purposes: the refutation of their saying, when the Prophet (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Harithah had divorced her, they said, "Muhammad has married his son's wife while he forbids people from that." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: the nullification of adoption (al-tabanni).

And that the truth lies in Allah's rulings, because He is the All-Aware of deeds, and He is the One who speaks the truth.

[Page 248]

And that the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the believers is a stronger authority, and that his wives have the sanctity of mothers for them, and that authority is by the appointment of Allah, so it is stronger and more binding than the authority of kinship.

And the encouragement of the believers to hold fast to what Allah has legislated for them, because He took the covenant concerning that from all the Prophets.

And taking heed from what Allah manifested of His care for the victory of the believers over the confederates of their enemies from the disbelievers and the hypocrites at the Battle of the Confederates, and the repelling of the plot of the hypocrites.

And the praise of the believers for their truthfulness and steadfastness in defending the religion.

And Allah's blessing upon them in giving them the lands of the People of the Book who supported the confederates.

And it moves from that to rulings on dealing with the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and mentions their virtue and the virtue of the family of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the virtues of the people of goodness among the Muslim men and women.

And legislation on the waiting period of a divorced woman before consummation.

Hukm (ruling) on the veiling of the Mothers of the Believers and on the dress of the believing women when they go out.

And the warning to the hypocrites for spreading false news (al-irjaf bil-akhbar al-kadhiba).

Interspersed throughout are digressions (mustatradat) on the command to emulate the Prophet ﷺ.

And the threat against the hypocrites who do that which harms Allah, His Messenger and the believers.

And the warning against becoming entangled in such conduct, lest they fall into what those who harmed Musa (peace be upon him) fell into.

They say, "When will this victory be, if you are truthful?" Say, "On the Day of Victory, their faith will not benefit those who disbelieved, nor will they be given respite." So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are waiting.

It is permissible for this to be coordinated with the sentence "then he turned away from it," meaning they turned away from listening to the verses and reflecting upon them, and they went beyond that to denial and mockery of them. The relevance of mentioning this here is that it came directly after the indication of the proof of the occurrence of resurrection, which is the Day of Judgment (yawm al-fasl).

It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with the sentence (﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]).

The meaning is that they denied the resurrection and what accompanies it of threats in the Hereafter, and they denied the threat of the punishment of this world, of which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21].

Al-fath (the victory) means help and decision. What is intended by it is the help of the people of faith through the manifestation of their success and the defeat of their enemies, for the defeat of the enemy is a victory for its opposite. The Muslims used to challenge the polytheists by saying that Allah would decide between them and would give them victory, and their proof would become manifest. So the disbelievers repeated their mockery of the Muslims by asking about the time of this victory, as a question used in denial, since what was asked about had not occurred.

The narration of their statement in the present tense serves to express astonishment at it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], along with conveying the repetition of this from them and their adopting it.

The meaning is: if you are truthful that it is going to happen, then tell us its time, for since you know of it apart from others, then you should know its time. This is from baseless sophistry, because knowing a thing in general does not require knowing the details of its circumstances, so that the one who does not know its details could be accused of lying in its general claim.

[Page 243 continues: the demonstrative in "this victory" (hadha al-fath), despite the possibility of dispensing with it by mentioning what explains it, is intended to belittle it and show little concern for it, as in the words of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"When this death comes, it will not find a need of mine
Except that I have fulfilled its fulfillment."]

This is an indication of his little concern for death. From it is His saying, exalted is He, reporting about them: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36]. So Allah commanded the Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them in the manner of wise discourse (al-uslub al-hakim), by saying that the true Day of Victory is the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day of Judgment, and at that time the hope of the disbelievers for salvation and for benefiting from regret and repentance will be cut off, and they will not find any respite to make up for what they have missed. That is, their benefiting from this admonition is better for them than their seeking to know the time of the arrival of the Day of Victory, because they will say on that day, ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us, and we will do righteousness; indeed, we are certain﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12]. Along with this answer is an implication that the time of its arrival is unknown to people and that it is among what Allah has kept exclusively to Himself. So whoever wishes to safeguard the salvation of his soul should act for it from now, for he does not know when it will befall him. Thus ﴿no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before or earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158].

In this answer, then, is the employment of wise discourse in two respects: in the respect of turning away from specifying the day of victory, and in the respect of turning them toward the true Day of Victory, whereas they had meant by victory the victory of the Muslims over them in the life of this world.

The mention of the description "those who disbelieved" in the place where a pronoun would have been expected, although they are the ones who said, "When will this victory be?", is for the purpose of recording against them that their disbelief is the cause of their defeat.

Then, following all these disputes and proofs, Allah directed His address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to turn away from these speakers who denied, and not to press them insistently, as a way of despairing of the faith of those among them who argue and who take the lead in deceiving their common people. This is a turning away of abandonment from debate, temporary and not permanent, nor is it a turning away from calling to Allah, and it has no connection with the rulings of jihad prescribed in other verses.

Al-intizar means waiting in anticipation. Its origin is derived from looking (al-nazar), as if it is the reflexive form of anzarahu, meaning he showed it to him so he waited, that is, he burdened himself to look.

The object of "wait" (intazir) is omitted for the sake of awe, meaning: wait for days in which there will be victory for you and in which there will be loss for them, like the years of famine if they occurred after the revelation of this surah, and like the Day of Badr and the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, both of which certainly occurred after the revelation of this surah. So in the command to wait there is an allusion of good news to the believers that they will look forward to it, and an allusion of threat to the polytheists of punishment in both abodes.

The clause "indeed, they are waiting" is a reason for what the command to wait contains of concealing punishment for them. The object of "waiting" (muntazirun) is omitted and indicated by the context, meaning: they are waiting for you to have an opportunity for your war or for your expulsion. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, we await for him the misfortunes of time"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30], and He said: ﴿And they await for you misfortunes; upon them is the misfortune of evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98]. That is, we were not unjust in determining punishment for them, because they were the ones who began with injustice.

Surat al-Ahzab

It is thus named (Surat al-Ahzab) in the mushafs, in books of tafsir, and in the Sunnah, and its naming has likewise been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b through acceptable chains. No other name for it is known. The reason for the naming is that it mentions the confederates (ahzab) of the polytheists from Quraysh and those who allied with them, who intended to attack the Muslims in Madinah, so Allah repelled their plot, and Allah sufficed the believers in fighting.

It is Madani by consensus. It will come that Ibn 'Abbas reported that the verse ﴿It is not for a believer﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36], etc., was revealed concerning the marriage of Zaynab bint Jahsh to Zayd ibn Harithah, in Makkah.

It is the ninetieth in the enumeration of the surahs revealed of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Anfal and before Surat al-Ma'idah.

Its revelation, according to the view of Ibn Ishaq, was at the end of the fifth year after the Hijrah, and this is what Ibn Rushd followed in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil. Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that it was in the fourth year, which is the year of the Battle of the Confederates (ghazwat al-ahzab), also called the Battle of the Trench (ghazwat al-khandaq), when groups from Quraysh, their Ahabish, Kinanah, and Ghatafan surrounded them, and they numbered ten thousand, while the Muslims were three thousand. Following it were the Battle of Qurayzah and the Battle of al-Nadir.

The number of its verses is seventy-three, by agreement of the scholars of counting.

Among what must be pointed out concerning this surah is what al-Hakim, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me, "How many do you count Surat al-Ahzab as having?" He said:

[Page 246]

I said, "Seventy-three verses." He said, "Aqat?" (with a hamzah of interrogation entering upon qat, meaning "is that all?"). "By Him by whom Ubayy swears, it used to equal Surat al-Baqarah. And we used to recite in it: 'The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, then stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise,'" so it was lifted in what was lifted, that is, it was abrogated in what was abrogated from the recitation of its verses. And what Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated with his chain, and Ibn al-Anbari with his chain, "from 'A'ishah who said: Surat al-Ahzab used to be recited in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) as two hundred verses, but when 'Uthman wrote the mushafs, he did not find of it except what is now." The wording of both reports is weak in chain.

The meaning of the first report, according to the scholars, is that Ubayy narrated about Surat al-Ahzab before some of it had been abrogated. Of it, some had its recitation and ruling abrogated, and of it, some had only its recitation abrogated, like the verse of stoning. I say: If what is attributed to Ubayy is authentic, then it is only that he used to attach much of the Qur'an to Surat al-Ahzab, though it belongs to other surahs of the Qur'an, like much of Surat al-Nisa', which resembles some of what is in Surat al-Ahzab in its themes and tone, of what mentions the hypocrites and the Jews. For the Companions of the Messenger of Allah did not follow one method in arranging the verses of the Qur'an, nor in the number of its surahs, nor in the division of its surahs, as was mentioned in the Eighth Introduction, nor in preserving the wording of what was abrogated. How, when the memorizers of the Qur'an, the four Caliphs, and all the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed, except for those who deviated, that the Qur'an is what is in the mushaf, and agreed on the number of the verses of the Qur'an to a figure close to one another, as was mentioned in the Eighth Introduction.

As for the report from 'A'ishah, it is weaker in chain and closer to interpretation. If it is authentic from her, and I do not think it is, then she spoke of something abrogated from the Qur'an that had been in Surat al-Ahzab.

After the consensus of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon the mushaf of 'Uthman, there is no quest for a seeker.

Their reliance regarding the quantity of the Qur'an and its surahs was only upon the memorization of the memorizers. Zayd ibn Thabit lacked a verse from Surat al-Ahzab which he did not find in the sheets of the Qur'an that had been handed to him, so he kept asking about it until he found it with Khuzaymah ibn Thabit al-Ansari, and he had been hearing the Messenger of Allah recite it. When he found it with Khuzaymah, he had no doubt about its wording, which he had known. It is the verse

[Page 247]

﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23] up to His saying "substitution." And he lacked the two verses at the end of Surat Bara'ah, and he found them with Abu Khuzaymah ibn Aws, who was known by his kunyah.

Finally, the report of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is a strange report, not transmitted from any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, so we are certain that a error entered it from some of its narrators. It is also a report of solitary transmission (khabar ahad), by which the consensus of the Ummah on the amount of this surah that exists, transmitted by mass transmission, is not overturned.

In al-Kashshaf: "As for what is reported that that addition narrated from 'A'ishah was written in a sheet in the house of 'A'ishah, and then a domestic sheep (al-dajin), that is a goat, ate it, it is among the fabrications of the heretics (al-malahidah) and the Rafidah." End of quote.

The fabrication of this report is clear and evident, for if it were true, this sheet would have perished in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) or after him, while the Companions were numerous and the memorizers of the Qur'an were many, so even if that sheet had perished, what was in it would not have perished from the breasts of the memorizers.

That the Qur'an has had much of it vanish is a foundational principle of the Rafidah, so that they may attack the three Caliphs with it. The Rafidah claim that the Qur'an is deposited with the awaited Imam, and that he is the one who will bring the Qur'an as a camel's load. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi thoroughly addressed their claim and fully refuted it in his book al-'Awasim min al-Qawasim.
